title: Is Jesus Yahweh? The Divine-Name Argument

keyTerms.d: Written with four Hebrew consonants, it was the personal name of the God who had spoken to Moses from the fire, and reverence for it ran so deep that a reader said Adonai, “Lord,” instead. That name belonged to God alone: “I am the LORD; that is my name … my glory I give to no other” (Isaiah 42:8).

The Greek word “Lord.” Exactly what the earliest Greek copies of the Jewish Scriptures wrote where the Hebrew had YHWH is genuinely debated, but the New Testament writers settle the question for their own usage: when they quote a passage where the Hebrew has YHWH, they write Kyrios — and they then take those very passages and apply them to Jesus.

Kyrios can mean “sir” or “master,” and not every “Lord” on Jesus’s lips carries the freight of the Name. The argument does not rest on the ordinary uses; it rests on the loaded ones — the places where a YHWH-text is quoted and turned on Jesus.

In the Greek of Paul’s Bible, Deuteronomy 6:4 carries two words for the one God of Israel, theos (“God”) and Kyrios (“Lord,” standing for the Name). In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul distributes them: the “one God” is the Father, and the “one Lord” is Jesus Christ. He has not added a second deity alongside the creed; he has reached inside it and placed Jesus within it — an influential reading, and genuinely contested.

Richard Bauckham’s phrase for including Jesus in the identity of the God of Israel. Influential but contested: James F. McGrath reads “one Lord” as set alongside the creed rather than inside it, and Hurtado, broadly an ally, frames the data as devotional practice rather than in Bauckham’s identity categories.

Second Temple Judaism knew of exalted intermediary figures — great angels, personified Wisdom, exalted patriarchs — with God’s authority, even his name, who were not God. But an agent has a ceiling: such figures characteristically refuse worship and redirect it to God. Agency conferred authority; it never conferred the Name and the worship together.

An “I am” with no predicate to complete it, as in “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). Its closest background is the LORD’s self-declaration “I am he” in Isaiah 40–55, which the Greek Old Testament renders with the very same absolute egō eimi (Isaiah 43:10). The tie to Exodus 3:14 is weaker and more contested, since the Greek there reads ho ōn.

An Aramaic prayer, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22), which Paul preserves untranslated in a Greek letter his readers already knew. Addressed to Jesus in prayer, it points back behind Paul’s Greek toward the earliest church. The consonants also permit maran atha, “Our Lord has come”; the imperative is the standard reading.

derive.q: Joel promises that “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” — where the Hebrew has YHWH. Paul quotes it of confessing and calling on Jesus (Romans 10:9–13). So the text…?
derive.ans: about calling on YHWH’s name becomes a text about calling on Jesus
derive.why: In Joel the Lord upon whose name one calls is YHWH himself. Paul takes a text about calling on the covenant name of God and, without a word of apology, makes it a text about calling on Jesus.

derive.q: Isaiah 45 — the chapter that insists “I am the LORD, and there is no other” — swears “to me every knee shall bow.” The Philippians hymn bends that oath to Jesus. So it is…?
derive.ans: not a second, lesser lord added — the one who bears this name is the LORD
derive.why: A monotheist does not do this by accident, and he does not do it with a creature. To take the chapter of Isaiah that most insists there is no god beside the LORD, and to apply its exclusive oath to Jesus, is not to add a second, lesser lord to the picture. That the hymn applies YHWH language specifically, rather than “Lord” more loosely, is itself contested among interpreters.

derive.q: The Greek Shema carries two words for the one God — theos and Kyrios. In an argument against idolatry, Paul writes “one God, the Father … and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” So Jesus is…?
derive.ans: placed within the creed, not beside it (influential, contested)
derive.why: Paul has not added a second deity alongside the creed; he has reached inside it and placed Jesus within it. The reading is influential — and genuinely contested. What is not in doubt is that Paul does it in the middle of an argument against idolatry, where smuggling in a second divine power would be the very sin he is condemning.

derive.q: A Greek letter preserves, untranslated, an Aramaic prayer to Jesus its readers already knew — and Paul, who records his clashes with Jerusalem openly, records none over praying to Jesus as Lord. So the devotion is…?
derive.ans: primitive and Jewish, not late and Greek
derive.why: Paul was in contact with the Jerusalem leaders within a few years of his conversion, and he records his clashes openly — over circumcision and over table fellowship with Cephas himself; nowhere does he record any dispute over praying to Jesus as Lord. A formula his Greek readers knew untranslated, addressed to Jesus in prayer, points back behind Paul’s Greek toward the earliest church.

derive.q: Exalted intermediaries could carry God’s authority, but they refuse worship (“Worship God,” Revelation 19:10). Jesus is prayed to, called on, sung to, given Isaiah 45’s oath and written into the Shema. So the agency reading…?
derive.ans: hits its ceiling — it cannot bear the evidence
derive.why: An agent has a ceiling. The intermediary figures of Second Temple Judaism characteristically refuse worship and redirect it to God, whereas the first Christians prayed to Jesus, called on his name, and sang to him. No shaliach was ever given the exclusive oath of Isaiah 45 or written into the Shema. Agency conferred authority; it never conferred the Name and the worship together.

derive.q: Grant the whole pattern. Does it, by itself, prove the doctrine of the Trinity?
derive.ans: no — it shows what the earliest Christians confessed, and clears the charge of late invention
derive.why: It does not prove the doctrine of the Trinity from a single verse, and it does not settle, by itself, how the one God is Father, Son, and Spirit; that is the larger work of the doctrine of the Trinity. It shows that the earliest Christians confessed Jesus as the LORD, early and on purpose, and it clears the charge that his deity was a later invention.

honestState.p1: The reading that Paul reworks the Shema around Jesus — Bauckham’s inclusion of Jesus in the “unique divine identity” of the God of Israel, Wright’s Shema rewritten around Jesus — is influential and genuinely contested. James F. McGrath argues that Paul sets “one Lord” alongside the one God rather than folding him inside the creed; Hurtado, broadly an ally, frames the data as devotional practice rather than in Bauckham’s identity categories. Paul’s application of YHWH-texts to the Lord Jesus is catalogued in detail by David B. Capes; what those texts mean for Jesus’s identity is where the debate lives.
honestState.fairness: Several of the strongest divine-name texts are Paul’s, two of them in a single letter, so they are not, strictly, independent sources. What the earliest Greek copies wrote where the Hebrew had YHWH is genuinely debated — several pre-Christian copies preserve the Tetragrammaton rather than Kyrios. Whether the Philippians hymn invokes the Name specifically is debated, and the tie of John 8:58 to Exodus 3:14 is the weaker link. And the popular argument that echad in the Shema means a “compound” unity is a discredited overreach the case does not use.
honestState.verdict: The earliest Christians — monotheists who would die before bowing to an idol — took the name their people would not pronounce, and the Scriptures that name its bearer as the only God, and gave both to a crucified man, early, some of it in Aramaic, and on purpose. That is not the reverence owed a great teacher, or even a supreme angel; in a Jew it is a claim about the identity of God himself. And we hold that the confession is true: Jesus is the LORD — not a second god beside YHWH, and not the Father under another name, but the Son who shares the one divine Name with the Father; fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. This argument does not prove all of that. It shows that the earliest Christians confessed Jesus as the LORD, and it clears the charge that his deity was a later invention.

order: Where the Hebrew has YHWH, the New Testament writers write Kyrios — and apply those very texts to Jesus.
This is inclusion within the one God, not a second deity — and it is early and Jewish.
Therefore the New Testament identifies Jesus with YHWH, early and by design.

props.t: YHWH-texts quoted and turned on Jesus
Isaiah 45’s exclusive oath applied to Jesus
given the name that is above every name
an Aramaic prayer pointing back toward the earliest church
distinguished from the Father while sharing the one divine Name
rests on echad meaning a compound unity

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: Where Israel’s Scriptures have the divine name YHWH, the New Testament writers write Kyrios (“Lord”) — and they take those very texts and apply them to Jesus. Limit: not every “Lord” carries the Name; the case rests on the loaded uses, where a YHWH-text is quoted and turned on Jesus — not on the discredited echad word-play.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and what it does not claim.
cards.a: This is inclusion within the one God, not a second deity: Paul reworks the Shema itself, placing Jesus inside Israel’s creed — and it is early and Jewish, an Aramaic prayer to Jesus pointing back behind Paul’s Greek. It does not claim the Shema reading is uncontested; it is influential and genuinely contested.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the New Testament identifies Jesus with YHWH, giving him the divine Name and the Scriptures that belong to its bearer alone, early and by design. It does not prove the doctrine of the Trinity from a single verse, nor settle how the one God is Father, Son, and Spirit — that is the further work of the doctrine of the Trinity.

cards.q: Is Jesus, then, the Father under another name — or a second god?
cards.a: Neither. The New Testament does this without confusing Jesus with the Father: “one God, the Father … and one Lord, Jesus Christ.” Jesus is the LORD — not a second god beside YHWH, and not the Father under another name, but the Son who shares the one divine Name with the Father.

cards.q: Why does the case not rest on the Hebrew word echad?
cards.a: Because the “compound unity” argument proves far less than its enthusiasts suppose: the plurality in “one flesh” comes from the noun, not from echad, which is simply the ordinary Hebrew numeral “one” and routinely describes things that are emphatically singular. The case rests on something much harder to wave away: what the New Testament writers actually do with the divine name.

cards.q: What is the honest hedge on Kyrios as the rendering of YHWH — and why does the argument survive it?
cards.a: What the earliest Greek copies wrote, and what was said aloud, is genuinely debated: several pre-Christian copies preserve the Tetragrammaton rather than Kyrios. But the load-bearing fact is what the New Testament writers do on the page: where the Hebrew has YHWH they write Kyrios, and they apply that passage to Jesus.

cards.q: What move recurs across the pattern’s source texts?
cards.a: A text that belongs to YHWH alone is redirected to Jesus: calling on the name of the LORD becomes calling on Jesus (Romans 10:13); the exclusive oath “to me every knee shall bow” becomes bowing at the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11); “honor the LORD of hosts as holy” becomes “honor Christ the Lord as holy” (1 Peter 3:15); a hymn to the eternal Creator is spoken by the Father to the Son (Hebrews 1:10–12).

cards.q: Why is the choice of Isaiah 45 so telling?
cards.a: Because it is one of the most fiercely monotheistic chapters in all of Scripture — “I am the LORD, and there is no other.” To take the chapter that most insists there is no god beside the LORD and apply its exclusive oath to Jesus is not to add a second, lesser lord to the picture; it is to say that the one who bears this name is the LORD.

cards.q: What does “the name that is above every name” point to — and how firmly?
cards.a: In a Jewish frame there is only one name above every name: the Name itself. The gift at the exaltation is not a promotion to high rank among creatures but the disclosure that the name he bears — Kyrios — is the divine one. Whether the hymn invokes the Name specifically, rather than “Lord” more loosely, is debated; the phrase points that way.

cards.q: Why does it matter that 1 Corinthians 8:6 sits in an argument against idolatry?
cards.a: Because smuggling in a second divine power would be the very sin Paul is condemning. Set against the pagan world’s many “gods” and many “lords,” his “one God … one Lord” distributes the Shema’s two words for the one God rather than adding a second deity — a reading that is influential and genuinely contested.

cards.q: “Before Abraham was, I am” — what is its closest background, and which link is weaker?
cards.a: The LORD’s self-declaration “I am he” in Isaiah 40–55, which the Greek Old Testament renders with the very same absolute egō eimi — and the hearers pick up stones. The tie to the burning bush (Exodus 3:14) is weaker, since the Greek there reads ho ōn. Even read as “I have been,” the saying claims existence before Abraham; and the divine-name case rests on the earlier Pauline material, not on John.

cards.q: “It’s all built on one creative theologian” — what is granted, and what answers it?
cards.a: Granted: several of the strongest texts are Paul’s, two in a single letter, so they are not strictly independent sources. But the material is not all of one kind or all from Paul: a fixed liturgical prayer, scriptural citations, a creedal reformulation, the Petrine reworking of Isaiah 8, Hebrews’ use of Psalm 102, and the Johannine “I am” — at least two of these are widely judged to be tradition Paul inherited rather than coined.

obj.q: Kyrios is an everyday Greek word — “sir,” “master.” Calling Jesus “Lord” no more makes him God than calling a landowner “lord” does.
obj.model: Granted, and the argument concedes it: not every “Lord” on Jesus’s lips carries the freight of the Name. The case rests only on the loaded uses — the places where the New Testament quotes a text about YHWH and turns it on Jesus: Joel’s “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD” becomes calling on Jesus; Isaiah 45’s exclusive oath, in the chapter that says “I am the LORD, and there is no other,” becomes every knee bowing at the name of Jesus. He is given “the name that is above every name,” and he is prayed to. It is the transfer of YHWH’s own texts, not the bare word “Lord,” that does the work.

obj.q: Judaism knew exalted intermediaries — great angels, personified Wisdom, exalted patriarchs — with God’s authority, even his name, who were not God. Jesus is God’s supreme agent, carrying the Name as an ambassador carries his king’s.
obj.model: This must be met on its merits, and the sending-language can be granted; the reading still has a ceiling. The intermediary figures of Second Temple Judaism characteristically refuse worship and redirect it to God — “Worship God,” cries the angel in Revelation 19:10 — whereas the first Christians prayed to Jesus, called on his name, and sang to him. No shaliach was ever given the exclusive oath of Isaiah 45 or written into the Shema. Agency conferred authority; it never conferred the Name and the worship together. An ambassador speaks for the king; he does not receive the king’s own exclusive oath and prayers. So the agency reading does not hold.

obj.q: Worship of Jesus as “Lord” was a late, Greek development — it arose in the Gentile churches, surrounded by the “lords” of pagan cult, not among the first Aramaic-speaking disciples.
obj.model: The most damaging reply is a single Aramaic word. Writing in Greek to Corinth in the early 50s, Paul preserves untranslated a prayer his readers already knew: Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” It can be replied that the Kyrios-cult arose in bilingual Syrian centres where Aramaic was spoken alongside Greek. But Paul was in contact with the Jerusalem leaders within a few years of his conversion, and he records his clashes openly — over circumcision, and over table fellowship with Cephas himself; nowhere does he record any dispute over praying to Jesus as Lord. A formula addressed to Jesus in prayer and never, so far as Paul records, disputed by Jerusalem points back toward the earliest church. The devotion is primitive and Jewish, not late and Greek.

obj.q: 1 Corinthians 8:6 sets “one Lord” alongside the one God, not inside the creed. Jesus is the exalted Messiah, a distinct figure next to God.
obj.model: This objection has a factual kernel, and the kernel should be granted precisely: the verse is genuinely contested. But the word Kyrios creates a dilemma for the “alongside” reading. In the Shema Paul is echoing, Kyrios is the creed’s own divine title. So if “one Lord” names a being who is not the one God, Paul has confessed — in an argument against idolatry — one God plus a second divine power “through whom are all things,” which is exactly what the objection set out to avoid. The reading that keeps monotheism is the one that includes Jesus, distinct from the Father, within the one divine identity both of the creed’s titles name. Jesus is not the Father under another name, and not a second god beside him, but the Son who shares the one divine Name with the Father.

unseen.q: Hebrews 1:10 only works because of the Greek. The “Lord” it addresses comes from the Septuagint of Psalm 102; strip the translation and there is no divine-name text being turned on Jesus at all.
unseen.model: Grant that Hebrews quotes the psalm from the Greek, where the Son is addressed as “Lord.” The force does not hang on that word: Psalm 102 is a hymn addressed to the eternal Creator — “you… laid the foundation of the earth” — and Hebrews puts it on the Father’s lips as words spoken to the Son. Nor does the case stand on one verse: whether any single verse quotes the Name specifically can be debated case by case; the pattern across them — Joel in Romans 10, Isaiah 45 in Philippians 2, Isaiah 8 in 1 Peter 3:15 — is deliberate and hard to explain otherwise. Jesus is not the Father under another name, and not a second god beside him, but the Son who shares the one divine Name with the Father.
